specialSection: Page-by-page comparison shows that Pages 1-5 of the earlier version and Pages 1-5 of the UPDATE contain the same core academic material. The UPDATE adds Page 6 on the eigenvalue cliff, cumulative variance explained, and dimensionality cutoff. No unique formula or argument from the earlier version needs separate retention.
synthesis: The common and difference eigenmodes of a symmetric two-neuron network can be calculated completely by hand: one receives feedback +w0 and the other −w0. If the difference mode decays rapidly, the neural trajectory collapses toward the common-mode line and becomes approximately one-dimensional. PCA does not require W; it finds maximum projected variance from centered activity covariance. Dynamical eigenvectors of W can relate to principal components of C, but they are not generally identical.
commonTraps: Equating eigenvectors of W with covariance PCs without additional assumptions.
Omitting \(1/\sqrt 2\) when normalizing the common and difference modes.
Using the wrong ± sign in the mode time constants.
Misreading a low-dimensional trajectory as activity in only a few neurons.
Applying PCA without centering the data.
Treating maximum variance as maximum causal or behavioral relevance.
Treating the eigenvalue cliff as an objectively unique dimensionality cutoff.
The UPDATE is the primary version and adds Page 6. PCA orders directions by variance; it does not automatically discover causal dynamics and can mix signal, noise, and condition structure.

synthesis: Whether rhythm persists after synaptic block can distinguish candidate intrinsic-pacemaker and network-generated mechanisms. Complex eigenvalues in a linear two-neuron system produce only damped or growing oscillatory components; a stable autonomous limit cycle requires nonlinearity. Fast voltage and slow recovery nullclines in Morris–Lecar generate a relaxation oscillation, while a mutually inhibitory half-center can alternate through intrinsic release or escape.
commonTraps: Calling every rhythmic activity pattern a CPG.
Assuming complex eigenvalues automatically imply sustained oscillation.
Ignoring the real part of the full eigenvalue.
Treating a nullcline as a trajectory.
Assuming a fixed point is stable merely because a nullcline intersection exists.
Distinguishing release from escape by superficial firing order rather than the intrinsic transition that triggers the switch.
Excluding sensory feedback from real locomotor rhythms.
Avoid classifying all rhythmic activity as a CPG, and do not conflate a damped linear oscillation with an autonomous nonlinear oscillator.

synthesis: The oculomotor integrator must retain eye position after a saccade, so the network needs a long-time-scale mode near \(\lambda =1\). For a general \(2\times 2\) W, perfect integration imposes only \(\det(I-W)=0\), leaving a many-to-one family of weights; parameter degeneracy is still stronger in complex biological models. Once measured tuning and synaptic nonlinearities are fixed, fitting can be rewritten as linear regression. Hessian eigenvalues separate a few stiff combinations from many sloppy ones, motivating an adequate-model ensemble rather than a unique best fit.
commonTraps: Mistaking persistent eye position for a sensory afterimage rather than an integral of velocity.
Requiring \(\lambda =1\) but failing to check stability of the other modes.
Using the division-based family formula even when \(W_{12}=0\).
Treating a many-to-one parameter mapping as measurement noise.
Confusing low dimensionality in neural-state space with sloppiness in parameter space.
Interpreting a sloppy parameter as biologically irrelevant.
Reporting only best-fit weights without uncertainty or an ensemble.
Low dimensionality in neural-state space and sloppiness in parameter space must be distinguished; they are different ideas in different spaces.

synthesis: Directional tuning is a classic description of motor cortex, whereas the modern population view asks whether low-dimensional trajectories generate movement dynamics. GPFA embeds smooth latent factors into noisy neural activity with a Gaussian observation model and explicitly models temporal covariance. A preparatory state can vary within the null space of muscle readout U without causing movement. BMI decodes neural or latent state into device commands and uses feedback and cross-day latent alignment to improve stability.

synthesis: Learned decisions must connect stimulus/action activity to delayed reward. A simple reward-gated Hebbian rule keeps strengthening when reward is common; subtracting the expected-reward baseline turns it into a covariance rule. Under a specified choice model and assumptions, the stationary covariance condition produces matching behavior. Rescorla–Wagner learns cue value from current reward-prediction error, while TD extends error to future value. Dopamine cue-transfer and omission patterns resemble RPE, though dopamine signals may also mix salience and movement.

synthesis: The central MDP claim is not that the environment has no history, but that the chosen state representation makes the future conditionally independent of earlier history given current state and action. Discounted return decomposes recursively into immediate reward plus \(\gamma\) times future return, yielding the Bellman optimality equation. Q-learning uses a sampled Bellman error for an off-policy bootstrap update. Model-based RL also learns a transition/reward model and can improve sample efficiency with simulated experience or replay.
commonTraps: Equating the Markov property with an environment that has no history.
Omitting the transition expectation from the Bellman equation.
Using the behavior action in a Q-learning target and inadvertently writing SARSA.
Assuming that the random branch of ε-greedy samples only nongreedy actions without stating that convention.
Equating model-free learning with an absence of internal representation.
Equating hippocampal replay directly with an exact Bellman backup.
Q-learning is not a synonym for every TD-learning method, and hippocampal replay is not directly equivalent to an exact Bellman backup; evidence and inference must be distinguished explicitly.

synthesis: The Hopfield model abstracts explicit memory as attractor dynamics: recurrent updates drive a partial cue toward a stored pattern. Symmetric weights and asynchronous single-neuron updates ensure that Ising energy cannot increase. For \(P=1\), Hebbian weights make both the target and its sign-reversed pattern fixed points. For \(P>1\), the other memories produce crosstalk noise; as loading \(\alpha =P/N\) rises, retrieval errors increase, and stable retrieval disappears near \(\alpha \approx 0.138\) in the classic dense random model.

Calling only \(\xi\) an attractor for \(P=1\) while overlooking \(-\xi\) and the spurious states implied by global sign symmetry.
Conflating overlap with exact bit accuracy.
Failing to check how crosstalk variance scales with N and P.
Treating the Gaussian approximation as an exact finite-N law.
Treating 0.138N as the memory capacity of the brain.

Failing to state that a 'memory capacity of 0.138N' refers only to the stable-retrieval criterion of the classic dense random-pattern Hopfield model, not to a conclusion about biological memory capacity.

synthesis: Systems consolidation changes both the anatomical dependence and the psychological character of memory: recent memories tend to be more vivid and episodic, whereas remote memories tend to be more gist-like and semantic. In the Teacher–Student–Notebook framework, the environment or Teacher is a generative source, the neocortical Student slowly learns predictive structure, and the hippocampal Notebook rapidly stores and replays one-shot episodes. Continuous standard transfer can also write unpredictable noise into the Student and thereby impair generalization. Go-CLS instead controls transfer according to signal predictability/SNR and stops at the optimum, so unpredictable episodic detail remains hippocampus-dependent.
commonTraps: A single case such as patient E.P. cannot establish every mechanism of consolidation.
Recent memory is not absolutely equivalent to hippocampal storage, nor is remote memory absolutely equivalent to neocortical storage.
A correlation with replay does not by itself demonstrate causal synaptic transfer.
Teacher, Student, and Notebook are formal roles rather than one-to-one anatomical labels.
Memory error and generalization error are distinct metrics.
Lower training error does not necessarily mean that consolidation is better.
Go-CLS predictions are not established facts.

Empirical observations, standard theory, the Teacher–Student–Notebook formal model, and Go-CLS predictions must be distinguished clearly, and model predictions must not be presented as established facts.
